title: The strange power of salt
text: Salt is so cheap today — pennies for a kilo — that its history reads like fantasy. For most of the past, it served as {{1}} (CURRENT), wage and treasury combined: Roman soldiers received a salt allowance, the possible origin of the word 'salary', and governments balanced their budgets on the {{2}} (PROCEED) of state salt monopolies. China nationalised production over two thousand years ago, with remarkable {{3}} (FORESEE), since salt is one of the few commodities everyone must buy. France's infamous gabelle taxed it so harshly that smuggling flourished, and the galleys filled with peasants whose offence strikes us as wholly {{4}} (PROPORTION). The tax also helped spark revolution. Nothing displays salt's political charge better than Gandhi's Salt March of 1930: 240 miles on foot to the sea, a handful of defiant crystals raised from the foam, and a colonial administration left looking stiff, brutal and faintly {{5}} (RIDICULE). Within seventeen years, salt had taken on an almost {{6}} (MYTH) status in the story of Indian independence. The white gold is now ordinary, yet its past remains a striking {{7}} (ILLUSTRATE) of how everyday things can acquire extraordinary {{8}} (SIGNIFY).

gaps.explanation: 'served as currency' — the noun of this family is currency.
'the proceeds of state monopolies' — plural noun from proceed.
'offence strikes us as wholly disproportionate' — negative prefix dis-.
'stiff, brutal and faintly ridiculous' — adjective from ridicule.
'an almost mythical status' — adjective from myth.
'a striking illustration of' — noun from illustrate.
